title: Carrying the sutra (section 15)
hookLine: one who keeps and explains this sutra carries awakening on their shoulders

lines: A STRAP, A CHILD, A BOX.
cards: A backpack strap digs into one shoulder. A toddler rides on a parent's shoulders at a parade, gripping two fistfuls of hair. A friend says, I've got this one, and takes the heavier box up the stairs.
Shoulders are where we put what matters enough to haul. After all its talk of giving and merit, section fifteen of the Diamond Sutra reaches for that same part of the body.
The people who keep this teaching, the Buddha says, carry awakening on their shoulders.

teach.b: First, the scale. Someone gives up their own body as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, in the morning, again at noon, again in the evening, age after age.
Someone who simply hears this teaching and trusts it, without turning against it, the Buddha says, has more merit than that. Second, the ladder. Hearing and trusting is the first rung.
Then come those who copy it out, keep it, recite it, and explain it to others: from the ear, to the hand, to the mouth, to another person.
Keeping isn't storing a book on a shelf; it's holding the words close enough that they get used.
This sutra, the Buddha says, is spoken for those who have set out on the great vehicle, the path of awakening for the sake of everyone. Third, the shoulders.
The Tathagata knows and sees such people, and they carry his awakening on their shoulders.
Awakening, in that picture, isn't a private prize; it's a weight that gets passed along, the way a family carries a recipe or a trade.
The sutra adds a warning, in the sharp language of an old argument between schools: those who delight in lesser teachings, and cling to the idea of a self, can't really hear this one.
That's the sutra's claim, not a verdict on anyone. Fourth, the paradox.
A sutra about not grasping now asks to be carried.

Some readers find the point right there: you can carry something without owning it. A parent carries a sleeping child in from the car and never once thinks, this child is my possession. The weight is real.

how: In some Mahayana communities the Diamond Sutra is copied by hand, recited aloud, and taught to others, which the sutra itself names as ways of keeping it.

games.why: the sutra climbs from hearing and trusting to copying, reciting and explaining; those who do so carry awakening on their shoulders.

practice: Let your shoulders drop, and pick up one line from the last few days, a mind that rests on nothing, perhaps, or beyond the marks.
Let it settle across the shoulders like a strap adjusted to fit, and walk through today in your mind, the commute, the dishes, the hard call, asking what the line would change.
Rest with the breath and the weight together, firm and light.

wordCard.voice: Carrying the sutra. In section fifteen, those who keep, recite and explain this teaching carry the Tathagata's awakening on their shoulders. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit for a teaching text like this one; the Pali form is sutta.

carryVoice: Your line: on your shoulders. Carried, never owned. Go gently today, and I'll see you tomorrow.
